title: Walden Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Walden wells have a 100 ft median depth, with local drilling and finished-well costs shaped by fractured mountain bedrock.
h1: What to Know About Wells in Walden, Colorado
intro_html:
Buying land near Walden means evaluating the well record as closely as the road, soils, and house site. Within five miles of town, Colorado DWR records show 253 permitted wells. Of those, 156 are recorded as constructed, 167 report total depth, and only 26 report a pump yield.

The local record points to generally moderate well depths and useful reported yields, but mountain bedrock can change quickly from one parcel to the next. Use nearby well permits to set expectations, not to guarantee what a new hole will produce.

sections.heading: Walden well depths vary across the mountain bedrock
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Walden is 100 feet. The middle half runs from 29 to 150 feet, so many wells are relatively shallow, but the spread is wide. The 90th percentile is 274 feet, and the deepest well in the record reaches 845 feet.

Depth records are nearly split between wells under 100 feet and wells from 100 to 300 feet: 46% are under 100 feet and 45% fall in the 100-to-300-foot range. Another 8% are 300 to 600 feet, while 1% exceed 600 feet. For a drilling bid, use the 100-foot median only as a starting point. Fractured granite and gneiss can produce water at different depths on neighboring lots, so ask for a written depth assumption and price per additional foot.

sections.heading: Reported yields near Walden are often workable
sections.html:
Only 26 wells report a pump yield, so the yield statistics are less complete than the depth records. Among those reports, the median yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half ranges from 8.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute.

Fifty-eight percent of reported wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute. Another 31% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Four percent report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, and 8% are under 1 gallon per minute. That under-1-gallon share is important for a buyer: a low-producing well may still serve a modest household with adequate storage, but it can limit irrigation, livestock, or future building plans. Confirm the test method, recovery, and storage capacity rather than relying on a nearby yield alone.

sections.heading: Shallow recorded water levels do not prove a stable table
sections.html:
The eight wells reporting static water levels show a median depth to water of 28 feet. The middle half is 23 to 45 feet below ground. Those figures can help a driller think about pump setting, casing, and construction, but the sample is small.

The permit history does not show a water-level series by decade, so it does not establish that the water table is dropping or holding steady near Walden. Static level also changes with season, pumping, recharge, and the local fracture system. Have the well tested after it has recovered, and ask for the recorded static level and pumping drawdown. A shallow water level is not the same as a guaranteed high-yield well.

sections.heading: Walden permit history shows several active drilling periods
sections.html:
Permits have been issued around Walden from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit year recorded as 2025. The strongest permit activity in the record was in the 1990s with 53 permits, followed by 47 in the 2000s and 40 in the 1970s. The record includes 29 permits from the 2010s and 8 from the 2020s.

The most active drillers listed are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 43 records; Stolns & Son Drilling (Stolns, Lewis B.), with 31; and High Desert Irrigation LLC (Hersh, Larry), with 11. These names can help when tracking down construction details, but an old permit is not a substitute for a current flow test, water-quality test, or inspection.

sections.heading: What a Walden well may cost to drill and finish
sections.html:
Local drilling is modeled for fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss, at about $65 to $100 per foot. At the 100-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone models to about $6,500 to $10,000.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $12,500 to $22,000 at that median depth. A deeper hole can raise the cost quickly, and the total can also change with access, casing, grout, difficult rock, pump requirements, and distance to the building site. Get the driller to separate drilling, casing and grout, pump equipment, trenching, electrical, and testing. A bid based only on the median depth may not cover a lot that follows the deeper end of the local record.

sections.heading: Walden buyers should check water quality and site constraints
sections.html:
Mapped environmental records within about 10 miles include 12 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 42 historic mine features, and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These records do not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but they are a reason to order a laboratory water test and review the well location against nearby environmental features.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible in fractured bedrock even where nearby wells perform well. Also check septic setbacks, drainfield soils, access for a drilling rig, electrical routing, and the distance from the proposed house. Domestic or household use accounts for 47% of the local permit mix, while stock use accounts for 21%. A Colorado DWR permit controls the allowed use; it does not by itself guarantee safe water or a successful new well.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Walden, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Walden is 100 feet. The middle half ranges from 29 to 150 feet, while the 90th percentile is 274 feet. The deepest recorded well is 845 feet. Nearly half are under 100 feet, but fractured mountain bedrock means an individual lot can require substantially more drilling.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Walden?
faq.a: The local model uses $65 to $100 per foot for fractured granite and gneiss. At the 100-foot median depth, drilling the hole is about $6,500 to $10,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $12,500 to $22,000. Deeper drilling and difficult access can increase the bid.

faq.q: Do Walden wells produce enough water for a home?
faq.a: Among the 26 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 8.0 to 15.0. Fifty-eight percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 8% report under 1 gallon per minute. The sample is limited, so request a current yield test and confirm storage needs.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Walden?
faq.a: Permit records do not establish that water is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, mapped records include 12 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 42 historic mine features, and 3 EPA cleanup sites. Test the specific well through a certified laboratory, especially before purchase, and review the result for household drinking use.

faq.q: Are there risks when building a home on a Walden well?
faq.a: The main risks are variable fractured-bedrock yield, a deeper-than-expected hole, water-quality concerns, and site conflicts with septic or access. Of 253 permitted wells, 156 are recorded as constructed, but only 26 report pump yield. Before building, verify the DWR permit, well location, septic layout, electrical route, drilling access, and the water test.
